message.reasoning:
I need to decide how to liquidate assets for a $750 rent payment.

Mortgaging both properties only yields $200, leaving a $134 shortfall. Selling houses is therefore mandatory.

Selling all 12 houses yields $300. Combined with the $200 from mortgaging both properties, I can raise $500 total. I must sell houses evenly to maintain even distribution across the color group.

I can raise $350 by selling 6 houses and mortgaging both properties. This leaves $16. I could also mortgage Ventnor and sell 9 houses for $225, leaving $21.

Mortgaging States and selling 11 houses yields $345, leaving $11. Selling more houses would raise cash but destroy my only weapon. The light blue properties at four houses are worth $400 each, which could hurt p2. I must survive future hits after paying the rent.

p2 owns a full orange monopoly and three houses on Park Place and Boardwalk. Their cash is $313, so after receiving the rent they will have roughly $1063. Liquidating everything would leave me $166, but keeping some houses would reduce my cushion while preserving rent threat.

Dropping one house from each light blue property would reduce rent to $270, $270, and $300. That is still too weak to threaten p2 with roughly $1000 in cash.

Any meaningful house sale destroys my kill potential on the light blues. Even a four-house Connecticut rent of $450 cannot bankrupt p2, who will have roughly $1063 after receiving the rent. My only winning path was p2 landing on those four houses while cash-poor. Now they are flush with cash and will be able to pay my upcoming boardwalk and park place rent.

Mortgaging both properties and selling six houses is the minimum destruction. This leaves two houses on each light blue property, reducing rent to ninety dollars each. I will have no threat left against p2. With only sixteen dollars remaining, I cannot survive their board. The only unmortgaged property is Baltic Avenue, which costs too little to threaten them.

I am checking which of p2's unmortgaged properties are actually rentable. Their orange and dark blue properties are death traps, but Kentucky, Illinois, and Short Line are unimproved and cheap. I also notice Indiana is mortgaged, so the red monopoly might not apply.

Unimproved properties are safe. Kentucky and Illinois rent is only $36 and $40, which I can afford. The Short Line railroad costs $50, also manageable. These squares are survivable.

I own Mediterranean Avenue, so I cannot claim the Baltic Avenue monopoly. Baltic rent is only four dollars, which is manageable.

The instruction says to declare bankruptcy only when cash cannot be raised or should not be raised. I am weighing whether to pay the rent now and stay in the game, or declare bankruptcy immediately.

I cannot rebuild the light blues to four houses. The bank only has two houses left, and p2 could buy them. Paying the rent now is the only way to stay in the game and hope for a lucky break.

I can only take one action per turn, so I will mortgage both properties first to cover the $200 shortfall. Then I will sell six houses to reach the remaining $134. The engine will ask again if I still cannot pay.

I realized the mortgage tool only accepts one property per turn, so I cannot mortgage both properties in a single action. I am weighing whether to mortgage Ventnor first for $130 or sell houses first to raise the bulk of cash immediately.

Selling all twelve houses and mortgaging both properties yields $500, leaving $166 after rent. Selling nine houses instead leaves $91, but one house on each light blue property still produces only $30–$40 in rent, which is too weak to threaten p2. The goal is to survive until I can rebuild or they go bankrupt.

I am now calculating my exact landing positions from Tennessee Avenue. I need to see which squares I will hit next and whether they are safe.

From Tennessee Avenue, a roll of two lands on New York Avenue. p2 owns four houses there for $800 in rent. That is an instant death trap. A roll of three lands on Free Parking, which is safe. A roll of four lands on Kentucky Avenue, where rent is only about $18–$36 and may be survivable depending on cash.

Only a roll of two from Tennessee lands on p2's New York Avenue, an instant death trap. The other squares are either mortgaged or unimproved and safe. The orange threat is therefore minimal.

I am now calculating the exact number of spaces between Tennessee Avenue and the dark blue properties. Park Place and Boardwalk are nineteen spaces away, so I could land on them within two or three turns. With only sixteen dollars remaining, any landing on those squares is a guaranteed death. I am weighing whether the extra cash from selling more houses would be worth the increased risk.

With only sixteen dollars remaining, almost every unmortgaged property is a death trap. Kentucky, Illinois, and Short Line all cost more than that amount, so I would die on almost any landing except Baltic Avenue. Selling all houses and mortgaging both properties yields one hundred sixty-six dollars instead. That extra cushion is enough to survive those same squares and luxury tax.

I am now certain that selling all twelve houses and mortgaging both properties is the only viable path. The extra seventy-five dollars from keeping one house each is not worth the reduced rent threat against p2's roughly one thousand dollars in cash. I will maximize cash now and leave the unmortgage cost for later.

I will not trade States Avenue or Ventnor Avenue. They need those to complete their pink and yellow monopolies, so keeping them mortgaged prevents them from building up a full set.

I will not trade Pacific or North Carolina to complete their green monopoly. The orange and dark blue monopolies already pose enough threat. Declaring bankruptcy now is a certain loss. Paying the rent and continuing offers a slim chance of survival.

I will sell all twelve houses first to raise the bulk of cash, then mortgage both properties in subsequent prompts. I will submit a sell_houses_or_hotel action with a plan to remove four houses from each light blue property, and I will keep my messages concise.

I will submit a sell_plan array with three entries, removing four houses from each light blue property. This raises $300, leaving a $34 shortfall. I must mortgage both properties before selling the houses, because the engine applies the mortgage and updates cash immediately, then asks again if payment remains insufficient.

I realized the engine may deduct the rent immediately once I can pay, which would prevent me from liquidating further. If I sell all houses first, then mortgage Ventnor, the engine might take the payment and leave States unmortgaged. The safer sequence is to mortgage both properties first, then sell the houses.

message.reasoning:
I need to decide how to liquidate assets to pay the $750 rent owed to player p2.

Cash is $546. The shortfall is $204. I can mortgage STATES_AVENUE for about $70. I could sell houses from ORIENTAL, VERMONT, or CONNECTICUT to raise the remaining $134. Selling buildings keeps properties unmortgaged.

Selling all 12 light blue houses yields $300. Combined with the $130 Ventnor mortgage, cash becomes $846 and the $750 rent is fully covered. Left with $96. Mortgaging States alone would still leave a $134 shortfall.

I am reconsidering whether to sell all houses. The prior plan of fully liquidating would leave $166, but only $204 is needed. I am weighing strategic value: p2 will have $750 after receiving the rent, which could let them pay even four-house light blue rent.

Player p2 will have $1063 after receiving the rent, so they can easily pay four-house light blue rent. Hotels are not a threat because I lack both hotels and enough cash to buy them. Nine houses must be sold to cover the $204 shortfall; eight would leave $4 short. I am also checking whether building rules require selling evenly.

Monopoly rules likely require even house counts. Selling nine houses would leave one on each light blue property, yielding only $30–$40 in rent. Selling six houses and mortgaging States instead leaves two houses on each, still covering the shortfall with extra cash.

Player p2 holds an orange monopoly with four houses on St. James, Tennessee, and New York. They also own dark blue properties with three houses each and several unmortgaged red and light blue properties. I am the only remaining player with a fully developed light blue set. This makes my houses a significant threat to them.

I am mapping the board to assess future danger. Player p2 owns an incomplete pink set with St. Charles and Virginia mortgaged, and an incomplete yellow set with Atlantic and Marvin mortgaged. I am calculating how many spaces remain until I land on their orange properties.

I mapped the full board order and am calculating next landing spots from Tennessee. A roll of 2 lands on Free Parking, while a roll of 3 lands on Kentucky. I am checking whether Indiana's mortgage breaks the red monopoly.

I am recalling whether a color-group monopoly still doubles rent when some properties are mortgaged. Standard rules suggest doubling applies only if every property in the set is unmortgaged.

I am uncertain whether a color-group monopoly still doubles rent when some properties are mortgaged. If it does, the doubled rent on Kentucky and Illinois would be only $36 and $48, which is not lethal. Indiana, B&O, and Atlantic are all mortgaged, so they yield no rent. Ventnor is also mortgaged, meaning I would not collect rent from it.

The next roll from Tennessee is relatively safe. New York is unreachable with a single roll, and the dark blue properties are fifteen spaces away.

I am safe on the next roll from Tennessee. I will pay the rent and end my turn. Player p2 will then roll from States Avenue, landing on Virginia, which is mortgaged.

Player p2's next roll from States Avenue would land on Penn RR, St. James, Tennessee, New York, Free Parking, Kentucky, Indiana, Illinois, B&O, and Atlantic. None of these are my light blue properties, since they lie behind them on the board. Neither player will hit the other's monopoly on this immediate turn.

Fully liquidating the light blue houses would reduce rent to roughly $12–$20, which is useless against a player with over $1000. Keeping four houses means they will eventually circle the board and collect $400–$450 in rent. Player p2 still has three houses on dark blue properties and enough cash to build more.

Player p2 could buy two more houses on dark blue properties to reach four total, raising rent to $1275 and $1700. They could also hotel an orange property, which returns four houses to the bank and frees up enough to build on dark blue.

Hoteling an orange property costs $100, the same as a house. Player p2 could use that to free houses for dark blue development.

Selling nine light blue houses and mortgaging States Avenue would raise about $370. After paying the $750 rent, cash would drop to $21. Remaining liquidity would be roughly $145.

Mortgaging States Avenue and selling six light blue houses yields the same total liquidity as selling nine houses. The maximum cash available after paying the rent is $166. Mortgaged properties cannot be built on and cost ten percent to unmortgage.

I am weighing whether to sell the light blue houses now or later. The maximum cash available after paying the rent is $166 regardless of timing, so selling them does not improve my ability to pay future debts. There is no penalty for waiting to sell buildings, and keeping uneven house counts might violate building restrictions.

I am now deciding between two liquidation strategies. Selling six houses and mortgaging States Avenue leaves two houses on each light blue property, raising about $220 and leaving a $16 surplus. Selling nine houses leaves three houses each, raising about $225 with a $21 surplus. I am weighing which configuration is more strategically useful.

Two houses on each light blue property would yield $90–$100 in rent, while three houses would yield only $30–$40. Four houses would generate $400–$450, which could be lethal if the opponent’s cash is low. Selling six houses would return eight to the bank, but player p2 might buy them immediately for dark blue development since only two houses remain.

Player p2 has $1063 and only two houses in the bank. Selling six light blue houses would return eight to the bank, allowing them to immediately build two more houses on dark blue properties. That would raise rent to $1275 and $1700. This makes selling now a critical strategic decision.

Mortgaging States Avenue for $70 still leaves a $134 shortfall, so at least six houses must be sold. Selling only six returns fewer houses to the bank than selling nine, and keeps rent higher with two houses per property instead of one. I am now weighing whether States Avenue is worth keeping unmortgaged, since the light blue monopoly is not complete.

States Avenue is worth mortgaging. The $70 mortgage is cheaper than the $77 cost to unmortgage it later, and it cannot be traded away since that would complete the opponent's pink set. I will mortgage States, then sell houses to cover the remaining shortfall.

I am reconsidering whether to fully liquidate all assets now, including mortgaging every property, rather than splitting the action into two steps.

Player p2 can pay a single four-house light blue rent of roughly $400–$450 with their $1063 cash. They cannot cover three hits totaling about $1250, so they would likely sell houses after two consecutive light blue lands. They also retain mortgage capacity.

I now see that four houses would drain about forty-two percent of the opponent's cash, which could block dark blue hotels or further building. I cannot keep four houses; the best I can do is six total. I am weighing whether two-house rent is worth keeping those houses off the market.

Player p2 can already free houses by hoteling an orange property. A hotel on St. James returns four houses to the bank, so they do not need my light blue houses for immediate dark blue development. My holdings only block the immediate two-house purchase; they cannot permanently prevent them from building later.

The housing shortage is not a hard constraint because player p2 can recycle houses by hoteling an orange property. The real trade-off is rent threat versus cash position. Keeping six light blue houses gives the same maximum liquidity after payment, but it also creates a chance to collect $90–$100 in rent if the opponent lands on those properties first.

Houses carry option value through rent collection, and bankruptcy rules would liquidate them anyway if I cannot pay. The minimum required action is to mortgage States Avenue for seventy dollars and sell six light blue houses for one hundred fifty dollars, leaving two houses on each property to collect rent.

I will mortgage States Avenue first, then sell houses in the next round. Selling all twelve light blue houses now would leave me with ninety-six dollars after paying the rent, but it would also remove my rent threat entirely. Selling nine houses now would pay the debt immediately and leave twenty-one dollars, yet it would weaken my rent position by leaving only one house on each property.

I will mortgage States Avenue now. I will keep the public message brief and avoid revealing strategy. I confirmed the house sell price is twenty-five dollars and the mortgage value is seventy dollars. I also verified that Oriental, Vermont, and Connecticut each hold four houses.

messages.content:
You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

p2 is at $92 and will keep matching $1 bids. A $93–$99 win only nets $1–$7 after the $100 mortgage, which does not change Park Place/Boardwalk survival, while continuing this auction burns turns. Fold and keep the $546 liquid. Never give States.

Only p2 left; they have orange 4-houses ($750-800) and dark blues at 3 ($1100/$1400). My $546 cannot survive those even after selling all 10 light-blue houses (~$250) plus mortgaging States/Ventnor. Staying in jail is the win condition: rent still collects, they must keep moving from Mediterranean into Oriental/Vermont/Connecticut. Paying $50 forces me onto the board. Roll; 5/6 stay safe. Never give States.

Only p2 left. Orange 4-houses ($750/$750/$800) and dark blues at 3 ($1100/$1400) kill me even after selling all light-blue houses. Never give States.

Only p2 left. Orange 4h ($750/$750/$800) and dark blue 3h ($1100/$1400) kill $556 even after selling light-blue houses. Jail is the win condition: I still collect (Oriental 4h=$400 can force them to strip houses; they have $323 on Park Place). jail_turns=2; roll keeps me in on 5/6. Paying $50 only puts me on the board. Never give States.

Only p2 left, $323 on Park Place. CT 3h=$300 and VT 3h=$270 they can pay; 4h makes all three LBs $400/$400/$450 and lethal. Their next roll hits LB on 9/11/12 (7/36). Cost $100, net liquidity only -$50 after resale. I am on GO so my next roll is safe. No trades: never complete their pink/yellow/green. Hotels next if still legal — deeper shortfall strips more orange houses.

Only p2 left, $323 on Income Tax — they roll next, same square as me. LB hits on 2/4/5 (8/36). Oriental already $400; VT/CT at 3h ($270/$300) they can pay in cash. $100 makes all three $400/$400/$450, forcing mortgages or house sales before I roll. Do not hotel: returns houses and burns the $750 St. James survival buffer. Never trade States (completes their pink).

Only p2 left, both on Income Tax, they roll next. LB 4h hits on 2/4/5 (8/36) at $400/$400/$450. Do not hotel: $50 each only raises rent to $550–$600, which their $323+$360 mortgage capacity ($683) still covers, and it dumps houses into a 2-house bank so they can push dark blues to 4. My only next-roll death square is St James on 12 ($750); I can raise that later by selling houses and mortgaging States/Ventnor. No trades — States completes their pink. End turn.

Only p2 left, $323 on Income Tax; I am on CT with $406. Their roll hits LB 4h on 2/4/5 (8/36) at $400/$400/$450. Their non-building liquidity is $663 (Baltic 30, Kentucky 110, Illinois 100, Short Line 100), so one hit does not force house sales and a hotel ($550–$600) still does not. Do not hotel: costs $50, returns 4 houses into a 2-house bank, and they can already hotel an orange without bank houses ($950 > my $906 max liquidity). My max raise is $906, so I survive orange 4h ($750/$800) only by selling all LB houses and mortgaging States ($70) and Ventnor ($130); a hotel on St James kills me on a 7. No trades — States completes pink, Ventnor completes yellow. End turn.

Owe $750 to p2, short $334. Houses only yield $300, so I must mortgage too. Liquidate fully before the shortfall closes: Ventnor $130, then States $70, then all 12 LB houses $300. Left with $166. Keeping houses is worthless — after this rent p2 has ~$1063 and can pay even 4h LB. Never trade States/Ventnor. $166 survives their undeveloped rents; oranges and dark blues still kill.

I need to decide whether to sell houses or declare bankruptcy to cover a $750 rent shortfall.

I have $616 cash but need $750. All properties are already mortgaged, so I must sell houses to cover the $134 shortfall. I can sell up to four houses from ORIENTAL_AVENUE, VERMONT_AVENUE, or CONNECTICUT_AVENUE.

Each house sells for $25. I need to sell six houses to cover the $134 shortfall. All three properties currently have four houses each, so I must keep them evenly distributed.

Selling two houses from each light blue property will raise $150. That covers the $134 shortfall and leaves $16 in cash. Five houses would not cover the debt.

Two houses on each light blue property yield only $90-$100 in rent. The opponent can easily afford that. Four houses would force bankruptcy, but I cannot keep them. Selling all twelve houses would raise $300 and leave $166 cash after paying the debt.

Selling three houses from each light blue would raise $225 but leave only $91 cash after paying the debt. One-house rents are too weak to threaten the opponent.

I am now assessing whether I can hurt p2 enough to win. p2 currently holds an orange monopoly with four houses on St James, Tennessee, and New York. They also have a dark blue set with three houses on Park Place and Boardwalk. Their red properties appear unmortgaged.

I am on p2's TENNESSEE_AVENUE, which explains the $750 rent. After the minimum sale, I will have only $16 left. Any further rent to p2 would bankrupt me. I am weighing whether to sell all houses now for a larger cash buffer or keep two houses as a defensive weapon.

Selling all houses now would not increase total liquidity. The same $166 could be raised later by selling the remaining houses at $25 each. Keeping houses provides a free upside: if p2 lands on them and pays rent, I gain cash without selling anything.

I realized keeping houses would tie up the bank's only two remaining houses. p2 cannot build more on their monopolies without those houses, so selling them back would give p2 the capital to expand their holdings.

p2 can already buy the two houses needed to complete their dark blue set. I have no other monopolies to expand, so selling my houses would only give p2 more capital to build on their existing holdings.

p2 can upgrade their orange monopoly to hotels without needing bank houses, since four houses return to the bank when a hotel is placed. They also own the red monopoly through Kentucky and Illinois, though Indiana is mortgaged and would need to be unmortgaged first. Ventnor belongs to me, so p2 cannot build there.

I am on TENNESSEE_AVENUE and p2 is on STATES_AVENUE. I paid rent because I landed there. p2 will roll from States next. That position is 13, so they are past my light blue properties and must go around the board.

The opponent cannot land on my houses this turn. From States, a single roll would require 33 spaces to reach Oriental, which is impossible. The rent upside is not immediate. Denying bank houses remains strategically useful if they attempt to build later.

I will sell two houses from each light blue property. I will keep the remaining six houses off the market to deny p2 building capital. The bank has only two houses left, so returning six would let them expand significantly. I will not reveal this strategy in my public message.
